title: Empirical Integration of a Formal Network Verifier as an Oracle inside an LLM Generate–Verify–Repair Loop: A Preregistered Paired Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired within‑task experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) to test whether embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) loop increases detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated network configurations and improves bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation. Using a synthetic intent→configuration suite (N=270 tasks), gpt-5-mini as generator, and a Dockerized Kathará/Mininet deterministic validator/emulator as ground truth, we observed no verifier rejections: baseline accepted 270/270 (100%); guarded (verify → optional bounded repair) accepted 270/270 (100%); bounded repair was not invoked. Paired difference = 0.00 (paired bootstrap 95% CI [0.00,0.00], exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0; bootstrap resamples = 10,000, seed = 1729). The preregistered execution used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false), so a single generated candidate per task was evaluated under both arms; this preregistered design choice is the proximate cause of the degenerate observed contingency and is documented with full execution provenance (preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0; master prompt archive SHA‑256 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). We release the complete preregistration, execution traces, scoring JSONs, and per‑artifact SHA‑256 manifest to enable deterministic reproduction and targeted minimal follow‑ups.

sections.introduction: Motivation. Large language models (LLMs) can translate high‑level network intent into low‑level device commands but their stochastic generation raises safety concerns: syntactically plausible yet semantically unsafe commands can disrupt production networks. A pragmatic defense is a Generate–Verify–Repair (GVR) pipeline: (1) generate candidate configuration(s); (2) deterministically verify safety/correctness with a network verifier; (3) upon rejection, invoke a bounded repair loop that uses verifier diagnostics to guide corrected generation. Research question. Does embedding a deterministic network verifier as an oracle inside a bounded LLM GVR loop increase the detection/rejection of unsafe or incorrect LLM‑generated network configurations and improve bounded repair success versus single‑shot generation? Contributions. (1) A fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired experiment (study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1) with public‑grade provenance; (2) complete execution, verifier traces, and scoring JSONs (artifact hashes below) allowing deterministic reproduction; (3) a documented operational lesson: generation semantics (shared candidate vs independent sampling) can determine whether a verifier insertion is measurable under a given estimand.
sections.related_work: Generate‑then‑verify architectures have been proposed to control hallucination and enforce correctness in compliance‑sensitive contexts; the generate‑verify‑repair pattern is argued as a practical defense for stochastic generators (see the preregistered literature leads and GVR position papers, e.g., Rafael Cadenas, Convergent Correctness). Formal deterministic verification frameworks for network properties (NetKAT/weighted NetKAT family) provide decision procedures that can serve as oracles inside GVR pipelines (Suárez Acevedo et al.). Recent work on intent‑based LLM‑assisted NetOps and RAG‑anchored agentic systems motivate experiments that combine LLM generation and deterministic verification (OpenAlex records W4414359351, W4400072049, W4386722061). Our work does not invent new verifier technology; instead we evaluate the measurable marginal effect of inserting an existing deterministic verifier into a preregistered paired study and fully archive the resulting artifacts and traces.
sections.methodology: Preregistration. The experimental plan was preregistered and frozen before execution (preregistration JSON, study_id netverify_gvr_empirical_integration_2026_v1; preregistration SHA‑256 8ae7fbadf89e5d56671560e43f03c4a92ad5f8c9b8586ac8eb3cc3c8fa00a1c0). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (within‑task difference in proportion of verifier rejections/accepts). Design. Paired within‑task: Npairs=270 synthetic tasks constructed as 3 vendor syntaxes × 3 topology templates × 30 tasks. For each task both arms were executed: (A) baseline = single‑shot generation + accept/reject scoring; (B) guarded = generation, deterministic verification, and bounded repair if verifier rejects (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1). Crucial preregistered execution semantics. The frozen execution_contract set independent_condition_generation=false (shared_initial_candidate semantics) and initial_generation_calls_per_task=1: one generated candidate per task was evaluated in both arms. Model and generator settings. Declared generator: gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json SHA‑256 a40e96e212ab87da251ac0d6dbb75bc543afa13438b5a6b9ebd073597ffdd820); provider recorded as openai_responses. Verifier and emulator. Deterministic_netops_validator_v5 validated each candidate against an emulated ground truth (Dockerized Kathará/Mininet); validator produced a JSON trace with normalized_configuration, violation codes (if any), parsed_command_count, and final validity decision. Sampling and power. The preregistered power calculation assumed independent sampling per arm (independent_condition_generation=true) and targeted an MDE ≈ 0.10 with N=270. The preregistered execution used shared candidate semantics; this changes the estimand the power calculation targeted. This design decision is archived and visible in the execution manifest (execution/execution_manifest.json). Analysis plan. Primary test: exact McNemar two‑sided on discordant pairs; paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed=1729). All raw responses, verifier traces, scoring JSONs (execution/scoring/*.json) and the per‑artifact SHA‑256 manifest are archived.

sections.discussion: Interpretation of the provenance‑backed null. The observed degenerate contingency (zero discordant pairs) is the arithmetic consequence of two jointly executed, preregistered conditions: (1) shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) produced one generated candidate per task that was evaluated in both arms; and (2) the chosen generator settings and prompt produced verifier‑acceptable outputs for every task in the synthetic suite. Because the preregistered power/MDE calculation assumed independent sampling per arm, that power calculation does not apply to the executed run; the observed p=1.0 and CI=[0.00,0.00] are therefore conditional on identical generated candidates and cannot be taken as general evidence that verifiers are ineffective. Operational implication. The run documents a concrete boundary condition: when a generator (with chosen prompt/settings) consistently outputs verifier‑acceptable candidates and the paired design uses a single candidate per task, inserting a deterministic verifier and bounded repair does not change measured accept/reject outcomes. This is a methodological, artifact‑grounded lesson about estimand specification and sampling semantics rather than a general negative claim about verifier utility. Deterministic reproducible follow‑up recipe (artifact‑anchored). To test the original preregistered estimand under independent per‑arm sampling using the same harness and artifacts, change the frozen execution fields as follows (fields exist in the archived preregistration/execution manifest): (A) set execution_contract.independent_condition_generation=true so each condition obtains an independent stochastic generation; (B) set maximum_model_calls (or planned_model_calls) to 540 so the harness permits one generation per arm per task; (C) set a nonzero generation temperature (or supply explicit per‑call seeds) in execution/model_configuration.json to expose sampling variance; (D) optionally increase maximum_repair_calls_per_task > 1 to test bounded repair convergence. These exact field names and artifact paths appear in the archived preregistration and execution manifest and permit deterministic minimal‑parameter follow‑ups without inventing new artifacts. Threats to validity. Internal: the shared‑candidate sampling semantics changed the estimand relative to the preregistered power plan. Construct: synthetic task suite approximates operational patterns (shutdown→change→restore, make‑before‑break) but is not production heterogeneity. External: single generator (gpt-5-mini) and one verifier rule set; results do not imply generality over models, prompts, or verifier conservatism. Conclusion validity: zero discordant pairs prevent informative rejection of the preregistered null for an independent‑sampling estimand; the archived artifacts demonstrate the precise cause and enable targeted re‑execution under independent sampling.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired study integrating a deterministic network verifier into an LLM GVR pipeline and released a complete provenance bundle. Under the executed shared_initial_candidate semantics and the chosen generator/settings, the single generated candidate per task was verifier‑acceptable for all N=270 tasks so the verifier/repair path was not invoked; observed paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00,0.00]; McNemar p=1.0). The principal scientific lesson is methodological: generation semantics (shared candidate vs independent sampling) critically determine whether a verifier insertion is testable under a given preregistered estimand and power plan. We publish all execution and scoring artifacts with SHA‑256 manifests so others can deterministically reproduce the run and perform the minimal JSON field changes (independent_condition_generation=true, model_calls=540, nonzero temperature/seeds, optional larger repair budget) required to test the original independent‑sampling estimand.

limitations: Synthetic task suite and limited operational realism: results may not generalize to complex, noisy, adversarial, or production NetOps environments; emulator behavior can differ from heterogeneous production devices.
Single‑model evaluation: only a single generator (gpt-5-mini) was used; no claim of multi‑model generality should be inferred.

Generation semantics constraint: the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation=false) produced one generated candidate per task and thereby eliminated between‑arm stochastic sampling variance; the preregistered MDE calculations assumed independent generation and are therefore inapplicable to the observed execution.
Bounded repair budget: the repair loop allowed at most one repair call per rejected candidate (maximum_repair_calls_per_task=1); multi‑attempt repair strategies were not evaluated.

Verifier rule‑set sensitivity: a single deterministic verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) and rule set were used; different verifier conservatism or policy choices will change false‑accept/reject tradeoffs.
Emulator vs production gap: emulator‑validated safety does not guarantee identical behavior on production devices or multi‑vendor deployments.
